CrystalBall.title:
Read
the future.
CrystalBall.intro: In the Balkans, grandmothers read the future in coffee grounds, at the bottom of the ibrik. Here, the crystal ball takes over. Rest your hand on it.
CrystalBall.idle: Touch the ball. It already knows what's coming to your table.
CrystalBall.reveal: I see… soon, on your table,
dishes: sarmale, rolled in brined cabbage leaves
warm papanasi, crème fraîche and red coulis
a lamb shoulder, long marinade, seven hours on the heat
a roasted feta, orange and hazelnuts
a spoonful of charred aubergine caviar
a slice of pistachio cake, rose and lemon icing
a slice of cozonac, walnuts and raisins
a Danube-style sea bream, on a long Saturday

About.title:
Balkan
cooking.
About.p1: “IBRIK KITCHEN is not just a restaurant. It is a way of living, a way of being that breaks free of convention so that everyone can feel like themselves — the way we are in the Balkans.”
About.p2: Ecaterina Paraschiv, known to everyone as Cathy, left Bucharest at six, when her parents fled the dictatorship to start over in France. After years in tax law, she answered an older calling and began cooking the food she'd missed. The name comes from her grandmother: the ibrik, the little copper pot she brewed coffee in, and at the bottom of which she claimed to read the future. IBRIK, the café in the 9th, opened in 2018; IBRIK KITCHEN, on rue de Mulhouse, followed in 2019. She is the one cooking, and the place looks like her.
About.photoAlt1: Chef Cathy Paraschiv in the kitchen at IBRIK KITCHEN, Paris 2nd
About.photoAlt2: Copper ibrik on the flame for Balkan coffee, IBRIK KITCHEN, Paris 2nd
About.p3: Her cooking treats the Balkans as a crossroads rather than a border: sarmale descend from Turkish dolma, mamaliga answers polenta, coffee comes from Istanbul. The recipes of mothers and grandmothers — mici, papanasi — are reworked with a direct hand inherited from her painter father: strip away the superfluous until only the essential remains. With natural wines from Eastern Europe, and one quiet idea: the Balkans are home to everyone.

Menu.lead: The recipes of mothers and grandmothers, reworked with finesse: mezze, embers, slow-cooked, sweets. Three plates between two, shared. IBRIK coffee to finish.

Press.title:
They keep
coming back.
Press.q1: The sarmale is a love letter written in cabbage and smoke. We did not stop eating.
Press.q2: An act of memory. Ibrik makes a Bucharest grandmother's table feel inevitable, even necessary.
Press.q3: A papanași so tender it briefly cured a hangover and a heartbreak in the same bite.

Events.p1: In Romanian, petrecere means a party, a feast and the time spent together, all at once. That is how we welcome people.
Events.p2: Twelve around the long table or sixty across the whole room: we cook the way Balkan families cook for their own. Plenty, all at once, and nobody quite leaves on time.
Events.card2Meta: Up to 60 guests · full restaurant · custom menu with the kitchen
Events.card3Meta: Off-site catering · sarmale by the hundred · țuică by the case

Reserve.lead: Everyone is welcome. Even if the table is full, ask us: we can nearly always find you a seat.
Reserve.takeawayText: Eating at home tonight? The whole menu is also available to take away — drop by or give us a call to order.
Reserve.asideP1: Looks full? Call anyway: there is nearly always room for you.
Reserve.asideP2: Large parties, last minute, a birthday nobody planned: tell us, we'll make it work.

Faq.title:
Your questions,
answered.
Faq.lead: Address, hours, booking, vegetarian dishes, what to order: the questions people ask us most.

where.a: IBRIK KITCHEN is at 9 rue de Mulhouse, 75002 Paris, in the Sentier. Two minutes on foot from Sentier metro (line 3), five from Bonne Nouvelle (lines 8 and 9) and Réaumur — Sébastopol (lines 3 and 4). Phone: +33 1 70 69 42 50.

romanian.q: Where can I eat Romanian food in Paris?
romanian.a: At IBRIK KITCHEN, 9 rue de Mulhouse, Paris 2nd. Chef Cathy Paraschiv, who came from Romania as a child, cooks the Romanian and Balkan recipes of mothers and grandmothers: sarmale, mici, mamaliga, papanasi. The restaurant is open Monday to Saturday, lunch and dinner.

hours.q: What are IBRIK KITCHEN's opening hours?
hours.a: IBRIK KITCHEN is open Monday to Saturday: lunch from 12:00 to 15:30, dinner from 19:00 to 00:30. Closed on Sundays.

cuisine.q: What kind of food does IBRIK KITCHEN serve?
cuisine.a: Balkan food: Romanian first, and with it the Greek, Serbian, Turkish and Ottoman heritage that meets in the region. The recipes of mothers and grandmothers are reworked with finesse, bistronomy-style. To try: sarmale (brined cabbage stuffed with Angus beef), mici grilled over embers, chicken souvlaki, seven-hour lamb shoulder, and papanasi for dessert.

wine.q: Is there a Balkan restaurant with natural wine in Paris?
wine.a: Yes: IBRIK KITCHEN serves natural wines from Eastern Europe, chosen to go with Balkan food. The wine list runs to more than 40 references, with a wine of the month.

booking.q: Do I need to book at IBRIK KITCHEN?
booking.a: It is a good idea, especially for dinner and on Saturdays. Book online through Zenchef, by phone on +33 1 70 69 42 50, or by email at bureau@ibrik.fr. Looks full? Call anyway: we will always find you a seat.

vegetarian.q: Are there vegetarian dishes on the menu?
vegetarian.a: Yes, at every service. Mezze: charred aubergine caviar, roasted feta, courgette fritter with feta, fennel risoni. Mains: pepper stuffed with pilaf rice, BLKN Avo' Toast, and a vegetarian souvlaki with feta. Vegetarian dishes are marked V on the menu.

budget.q: How much does a meal cost?
budget.a: At lunch, set menus run from €25 (mezze + main, or main + dessert) to €33 (mezze + main + dessert). At dinner, à la carte: mezze €11 to €17, mains €14 to €33, desserts €11 to €14. Expect €40 to €55 per person, before drinks.

groups.q: Can we come as a group or hire the restaurant?
groups.a: Yes. The long table, masa mare, seats 12 to 24 guests from €58 per person, three courses to share. The whole restaurant can be hired for up to 60 people from €4,200. IBRIK KITCHEN also caters christenings and weddings. Write to bureau@ibrik.fr or call +33 1 70 69 42 50.

chef.q: Who is the chef at IBRIK KITCHEN?
chef.a: Cathy Paraschiv, born Ecaterina. She left Bucharest at six, when her parents fled the dictatorship, and built a career in tax law before leaving it to cook the food of her roots. She opened IBRIK, the café in the 9th, in 2018, then IBRIK KITCHEN, the restaurant on rue de Mulhouse, in 2019. She is the one cooking, and the place looks like her.

cafe.q: Are IBRIK KITCHEN and the IBRIK café the same place?
cafe.a: No. IBRIK KITCHEN is the restaurant, at 9 rue de Mulhouse, Paris 2nd: lunch and dinner, Monday to Saturday. IBRIK is the café, in the 9th arrondissement. Two separate addresses, from the same chef, Cathy Paraschiv.

order.q: What should I order on a first visit?
order.a: Three plates for two, shared. Aubergine caviar and roasted feta to start, sarmale or mici off the embers next, pistachio cake to finish. And an IBRIK coffee brewed Balkan-style, in the ibrik: allow 5 to 10 minutes.
